block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.n: A glass bell on an iron plate. Pump the air out with a hand pump next to it.

Holds a pressure (Pa). Starts at 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. A hand pump next to it lowers the pressure each stroke (down to 1 kPa); a Sprengel mercury pump takes it down to 0.05 Pa. Air slowly leaks back in through the greased seal (about 0.1 Pa per minute). You cannot see the pressure - use a mercury gauge.

19th-century labs used a glass bell jar ground flat at the rim and greased onto a flat plate. The outside air pushes the bell down with about 1 kg on every square centimetre, which is what keeps it sealed.
Large or hot chambers later became welded mild steel, and ultra-high vacuum uses stainless steel baked at 150-250 C so gas trapped in the walls comes out first. Here only the glass stage exists.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.p: Omitted: the grease on the ground seal (tallow [2-09]).
message.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber: You can't see air pressure. Hold a mercury vacuum gauge and right-click.
block.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pump: Magdeburg hemispheres: with the air pumped out, 16 horses could not pull them apart.

Otto von Guericke's air pump (c. 1650). Place next to a vacuum chamber and right-click with an empty hand: each stroke removes 20% of the air (chamber : cylinder = 4 : 1). It never gets below about 1 kPa (1/100 atm). Costs a little hunger.

Each stroke follows Boyle's law: the chamber air spreads into the empty cylinder, the valve closes, and that share is pushed outside. The pressure falls like 0.8, 0.64, 0.51... so the first strokes do the most.

The limit comes from dead volume: air left in the gap between the piston and the valve at the end of the stroke expands back in, and the leather packing leaks. Guericke reached roughly a few hundred Pa to 1 kPa. Better vacuum needed Sprengel's mercury pump (1865) and the diffusion pump (1915).
Approximation: the real cylinder was cast brass/bronze ([1-05] not implemented) - steel here. The leather packing uses vanilla leather (rubber [2-29] not implemented).
message.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pu: Place a vacuum chamber next to the pump.
Whoosh... the piston still moves easily (lots of air left)
Whoosh... very heavy - the air outside pushes back on the piston
It won't go lower - this is the hand pump's limit (about 1 kPa)
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum_ga: Air pressure equals the weight of 76 cm of mercury.

A closed-end U-tube of mercury (Torricelli's mercury column, 1643). Right-click a vacuum chamber: the difference in mercury height is the pressure in mmHg (1 mmHg = 133 Pa, 1 atm = 760 mmHg). Below 1 mm it can't be read by eye.
One arm is sealed with nothing above the mercury (the 'Torricellian vacuum'); the other is open to the chamber. The chamber gas pushes its side down by exactly its pressure in mm of mercury.

For lower pressures came the McLeod gauge (1874, compresses a sample of gas with mercury so it can be read), the Pirani gauge (1906, how fast a hot wire cools) and the hot-cathode ionization gauge (1916, built like a vacuum tube).
message.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum: The mercury levels are within 1 mm - too low to read (below %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Everything is inside the glass, but it is still full of air. Seal it on a sealing station.
Glass bulb + tungsten wire filament + iron wire grid + iron plate. With air inside, the hot filament would burn out at once. Put it in a sealing station next to a pumped-down vacuum chamber.
Approximation: grid and plate are iron (nickel [1-37] not implemented). The lead-in wires through the glass (platinum / Dumet wire, glass-metal seal [5-12]) are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note1: Add one more electrode to a light bulb and you can control the flow of electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note: Lee de Forest's Audion (1906). The hot tungsten filament boils off electrons; the plate collects them; a small voltage on the grid between them controls a large current - an amplifier. Part of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note3: Fleming's diode (1904) used Edison's discovery that a hot filament gives off current. De Forest added the zig-zag grid. Before transistors, every radio, telephone repeater and early computer amplified with tubes like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note4: De Forest's first Audions were 'soft' - gas left inside made them erratic. Langmuir and Arnold (c. 1913) showed that a hard vacuum (about 10^-4 Pa) makes tubes stable, which needed diffusion pumps and getters (the silver film inside a tube is the getter that ate the last gas).
Pump the air out of the bulb, then melt the glass neck shut.

Place next to a vacuum chamber (it is the exhaust manifold). Tube assembly + chamber at 0.1 Pa or lower + 500 W x 10 s (filament heated to drive out gas) -> triode vacuum tube. A hand pump cannot reach 0.1 Pa - you need a Sprengel mercury pump. Each tube lets some air back into the chamber (5% of the gap to 1 atm) - wait for it to pump down again.

Real tube factories pumped each bulb through a glass tube at its top, heated the parts to drive out gas, then melted that tube shut with a flame. The little glass tip on old tubes and light bulbs is where it was sealed off.

Gas hides in the metal and glass surfaces. While pumping, the filament is run hot and the plate heated (later by induction) so the gas comes out before sealing; finally the getter is flashed to absorb what is left.
Approximation: the sealing-off flame (gas burner) is represented by electric power.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Tungsten only emits electrons (thermionic emission) above about 2000 °C. At that temperature in air it burns at once: 2W + 3O2 → 2WO3 (yellow smoke). Gas molecules would also get in the electrons' way.

De Forest's 1906 triode, the Audion, still held some gas (a "soft" vacuum) and behaved erratically. Around 1913 Langmuir and others pumped tubes to a high vacuum and made them stable. The silver mirror inside later tubes is the getter (barium) that soaks up leftover gas.
block.semiconductor-lab.sprengel_pump.no: A pump that carries air away bit by bit with falling drops of mercury.

Place it next to a vacuum chamber and load 4 mercury: it keeps pumping every second (no power, mercury is not used up). It reaches 0.05 Pa; at 0.1 Pa or below the sealing station can seal vacuum tubes. Roughing to 1 kPa with the hand pump first is a little faster.

Mercury drops falling down a narrow glass tube trap pockets of gas between them and push them down like little pistons. With no moving parts and no dead space it reaches pressures about ten thousand times lower than a hand pump - though the mercury's own vapour (about 0.2 Pa at 20 °C) remains.

Invented by Hermann Sprengel in London in 1865; his first pump emptied a half-litre vessel in about 20 minutes. In 1879 Swan and Edison exhausted their carbon-filament lamps with it, so the filaments glowed for a long time instead of burning out. Crookes ran several in series to study cathode rays in his discharge tubes - a path that led to the discovery of the electron.
Not enough mercury (%s / %s). Right-click with mercury
No vacuum chamber next to it
Mercury drops are falling: pumping the chamber next to it (down to 0.05 Pa)
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.note: A pump that spins a rotor with a motor and pushes air out steadily. Place it next to a vacuum chamber.

250 W electric. Pumps the adjacent vacuum chamber down to 1 Pa (about 17 s from 1 atm). It can also pump a chamber beyond an adjacent diffusion pump (as its backing pump). Recipe: rotor + 2 steel + motor + 2 mercury.

In 1905 Gaede built a 'rotary mercury pump' that carried air in pockets sealed by mercury on a rotating part, turning the vacuum pump from a hand tool into a motor-driven machine. Oil-sealed rotary pumps followed soon after (⚠️ around 1907).

As the off-centre (eccentric) rotor turns, the space between it and the casing grows to draw gas in and shrinks to push it out. Sealing the gaps with a liquid (mercury, oil) is the key. The lab's 'hum' is this pump.
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.plac: Approximation: stage 1 (mercury-sealed). Gaede's rotary mercury pump also used a separate backing pump; here it pumps directly from atmosphere. The 1 Pa limit is a game value. Oil stages (castor oil, silicone oil) come later.
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.n: A pump that knocks the remaining air away with a wind of mercury vapor. No moving parts.

400 W heater. Place it next to both a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump (backing). It starts once the chamber is below 10 Pa and brings it down to about 0.004 Pa, where it balances the leak (high vacuum, enough for evaporation). Recipe: 3 soda-lime glass + 2 iron + 2 mercury + tungsten wire (heater).

In 1915 Gaede boiled mercury in an iron pot and blew the vapor through glass tubes: the diffusion pump. In 1916 Langmuir cooled the walls with water to condense the vapor (the condensation pump) and made it much faster. Now vacuum tubes and lamps could reach high vacuum.

A fast downward jet of mercury vapor knocks any gas molecules that wander into it downwards. At atmospheric pressure there are too many molecules and the jet breaks up, so a backing pump must lower the pressure first. From 1928, low-vapor-pressure oils replaced mercury [5-06].
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.p: Approximation: Gaede heated with a Bunsen burner (here an electric heater). The cold trap that stops mercury vapor drifting into the chamber, the cooling water and the warm-up time are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note1: A machine that heats metal in a vacuum into vapor and coats glass with a thin layer of it.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note2: 300 W electric (tungsten wire heater). Place it next to a vacuum chamber; it runs only while the chamber is below 0.01 Pa (needs a diffusion pump [5-05]), 20 s per run. Crown glass + silver nugget -> half-silvered mirror; lens + fluorite -> coated lens [7-22]. Each run opens the chamber, so the pressure rises a little. Recipe: 2 W wire + 2 iron + copper cable + soda-lime glass.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note3: In 1912 Pohl and Pringsheim evaporated metals in vacuum to make mirror films (there were earlier attempts). In the 1930s John Strong evaporated aluminum onto telescope mirrors, making mirrors that tarnish less. The aluminum wiring of 1960s ICs was made the same way.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note4: Leftover air scatters the evaporated metal atoms. The distance a gas molecule travels before the next collision (mean free path) is about 6.6 mm divided by the pressure in Pa. At 0.01 Pa that is about 66 cm, longer than the bell jar, so atoms fly straight to the substrate.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.place: Omitted: film thickness control (the later quartz crystal thickness monitor [8-15]) and sputtering. For now silver and CaF2 can be deposited (aluminum, chromium and others once their prerequisites exist).
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note1: A pump that spins a bladed rotor extremely fast to bat gas molecules away. No oil or mercury, so the vacuum stays clean.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note2: 6 aluminium + 2 steel + motor. 300 W. With an adjacent vacuum chamber, a running rotary pump next to it (backing), the chamber at 10 Pa or less and a precise ball bearing (grade 2+, right-click with a bearing), it pumps down to 1e-6 Pa.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note3: In 1958 Becker at Pfeiffer in Germany presented the turbine-type molecular pump (its ancestor is Gaede's 1913 molecular pump). It needed precise ball bearings to carry blades spinning tens of thousands of times a minute.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note4: The blade tips move nearly as fast as the molecules (hundreds of m/s) and knock them downward. With no oil or mercury vapor backstreaming to dirty films, most semiconductor tool vacuums became turbomolecular.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.place: Approximation: blade stages and speed are skipped. No cold trap (which would stop a diffusion pump's vapor).
item.semiconductor-lab.methyl_chloride.n: A gas made from methanol and hydrogen chloride. Raw material for silicones.
Silicone reactor: methanol + dry hydrogen chloride (alumina catalyst) → methyl chloride. 2 per metallurgical silicon.
CH3OH + HCl → CH3Cl + H2O, with both gases passed over alumina at about 300 °C.
Flammable and harmful to the nerves if breathed (GHS: flame, health hazard). Plants keep it in closed piping. It was once a refrigerant, dropped because leaks were dangerous.
item.semiconductor-lab.dimethyldichloros: A liquid: silicon with two methyl groups and two chlorines. Water turns it into silicone.
Silicone reactor: 1 metallurgical silicon + 2 methyl chloride (copper catalyst) + empty glass bottle → this (direct process). With distilled water → silicone oil + hydrochloric acid.
Si + 2CH3Cl → (CH3)2SiCl2. The 'direct process' found around 1940 by Rochow at GE and Müller in Germany independently. Most silicone is still made this way.
Even moist air makes it fume white hydrogen chloride (GHS: flame, corrosive). The real direct process also gives methyltrichlorosilane and others, separated by distillation.
Omitted: ⚠️ by-products (methyltrichlorosilane etc.) are not made; main product only.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicone_oil.note: An oil of linked silicon and oxygen that hardly evaporates. Used in oil diffusion pumps.
Silicone reactor: dimethyldichlorosilane + distilled water → silicone oil + hydrochloric acid. Material for the oil diffusion pump.
A chain of repeating -Si(CH3)2-O- (polydimethylsiloxane). Heat-resistant, hard to burn, low vapour pressure.
Found in shampoo, cosmetics and water-repellent sprays. ⚠️ Real diffusion-pump oils are silicones with benzene rings (phenyl groups, e.g. DC-704) that evaporate even less.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicone_oil.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ phenyl silicones for diffusion pumps are not made; one dimethyl silicone oil stands in.
block.semiconductor-lab.silicone_reactor: Makes silicone oil in three reactions. What you put in picks the reaction.

2 kW, 15 s each. ① methanol + dry hydrogen chloride + alumina (catalyst) → methyl chloride ② metallurgical silicon + 2 methyl chloride + copper (catalyst) + empty bottle → dimethyldichlorosilane ③ dimethyldichlorosilane + distilled water → silicone oil + hydrochloric acid. Catalysts are kept.
Silicones are organic compounds of silicon. Kipping studied them in the 1900s; the direct process of about 1940 made mass production possible.
During the Second World War they were rushed into production as insulation for aircraft electrics and heat-resistant oils (Dow Corning, 1943).
Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Water from ① is discarded. By-products and distillation in ② are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.oil_diffusion_pu: A diffusion pump that boils an oil that hardly evaporates instead of mercury.
1 kW. Like the mercury diffusion pump, place it next to a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump; it starts below 10 Pa. Reaches 10⁻⁵ Pa and leaves 30% each second (mercury: 50%) = faster.
In 1928 Burch in Britain replaced mercury with a low-vapour-pressure oil distilled from petroleum; in the 1930s Hickman at Kodak made the fractionating type. Steel bodies allow large pumps.

No poisonous mercury vapour. Some oil vapour still creeps back into the chamber (backstreaming), so turbomolecular pumps are used when films must be clean. Letting air onto hot oil scorches it, so cool it before venting.
Omitted: ⚠️ real oils are phenyl silicones or petroleum oils. Cooling water, baffles and warm-up time are omitted; ultimate pressure and speed are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.mercury_baromete: A glass tube of mercury stood upside down. Right-click to read the air pressure at its height.
Crafting: 2 soda-lime glass + mercury (the iron flask comes back) + 2 planks. Right-click for the column height (mmHg) and pressure (hPa). The higher you place it, the lower it reads.
Mercury stops about 760 mm up the tube with a Torricellian vacuum above, where its weight balances the push of the air. 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 1013 hPa.

Torricelli made it in 1643; in 1648 Pascal's brother-in-law Périer showed the column is lower on a mountain. The hPa of weather forecasts honours Pascal. Mercury vapour is toxic, so such barometers fell out of use.
Omitted: ⚠️ weather and temperature changes are not modelled. The height scale (1/e per about 8400 blocks) is a game approximation.

block.semiconductor-lab.oil_diffusion_pu: Place next to both a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump. Once the chamber is below 10 Pa it pumps to 10⁻⁵ Pa. 1 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.silicone_reactor: By combination: methanol + hydrogen chloride (alumina) → methyl chloride; metallurgical silicon + 2 methyl chloride (copper) + bottle → dimethyldichlorosilane; that + distilled water → silicone oil. 2 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.h: Place next to a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump, then connect power. The rotary pump must pump first. Nothing is used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.howt: Place next to a vacuum chamber and connect power. It slowly pumps the air out, and also backs diffusion and turbo pumps.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.howto: Place next to a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump, right-click it with precise ball bearings, then connect power. A clean vacuum without oil or mercury.
